prompt: Which definition of a **stateless** app server is correct?

options.text: It never reads or writes persistent data itself, leaving every database call to a separate tier.
It keeps no request-to-request data in its own memory, so any copy can serve any request.
It only handles safe, read-only GET requests, so repeating a request can never change anything.
It keeps sessions on its local disk instead of in RAM, so they survive a process restart.

explanation: Stateless means the server holds no data between requests that only it knows; state lives in the request or in shared stores. (a) is wrong: stateless app servers read and write databases all the time; stateless describes where state lives, not whether data exists. (c) confuses statelessness with HTTP method safety. (d) is still local state: surviving a restart does not help, because another server cannot see that disk.

prompt: On a fresh HTTPS connection using TLS 1.3, roughly how many network round trips happen before the server receives the request?

options.text: Zero (sent with the SYN)
One (TLS rides on TCP)
Two (TCP, then TLS)
Three (TCP, then 2x TLS)

explanation: TCP needs one round trip for its handshake and TLS 1.3 needs one more, so the request goes out on the third trip. (a) only applies to a reused connection (or 0-RTT resumption, a special case); a fresh connection cannot carry the request on the SYN. (b) is wrong: the TLS handshake starts only after the TCP handshake completes, so it adds its own round trip. (d) describes TLS 1.2, which needs two round trips; TLS 1.3 cut that to one.

scenario: You run 6 app servers with in-memory sessions and sticky routing. During each deploy, servers restart one at a time and support tickets spike: "I got logged out" and "my cart is empty".

options.text: Deploy during the overnight low-traffic window so far fewer users are mid-session when servers restart.
Move sessions and carts to a shared store such as Redis and turn off sticky routing.
Add more app servers so each rolling restart wipes a smaller share of users' sessions and carts.
Lengthen the session cookie lifetime so users stay logged in across the restart of their server.

explanation: The root cause is that the only copy of session state lives in process memory. Moving it to a shared store makes restarts harmless and removes the need for sticky routing. (a) and (c) shrink the damage but every restart still wipes real sessions. (d) changes nothing: the cookie still points at session data that was wiped from memory.

prompt: Which of these are **naturally stateful** components? Select all that apply.

options.text: A PostgreSQL primary
A WebSocket server holding open chat connections
A REST API server that reads sessions from Redis
A Redis cache

explanation: Databases and caches exist to hold state, and an open WebSocket connection is state that cannot move to another machine. (c) is the textbook stateless server: its state lives in Redis, so any copy can serve the request.

prompt: What is the main drawback of putting a self-contained JWT on the client instead of a session id?

options.text: Servers cannot verify it without a database lookup.
It is hard to revoke before it expires.
It cannot carry a user id.
It only works with sticky sessions.

explanation: A signed token stays valid until expiry unless you add a server-side deny list, which reintroduces shared state. (a) is backwards: the point of a JWT is verifying without a lookup. (c) is false; user id is the usual claim. (d) is false; any server with the key can verify it.

scenario: Your app peaks at 3,000 requests per second. Every request reads the user's session. Sessions are 1 KB and there are 500,000 active sessions. The primary database already runs at 70% CPU.

options.text: In the primary database, in a sessions table.
In a replicated Redis session store.
In each app server's memory with sticky routing.
In an unsigned cookie.

explanation: 500,000 × 1 KB is about 500 MB, which fits in one Redis node, and 3,000 reads per second is trivial for Redis. (a) adds 3,000 queries per second to a database that is already busy, the hardest tier to scale. (c) brings back lost sessions on restart and skewed load. (d) lets users edit their own session.

prompt: Why does statelessness make autoscaling simple?

options.text: Stateless servers use much less CPU and memory, so each box can absorb more traffic.
Adding or removing a server neither requires moving data nor loses any.
Stateless servers need no load balancer, since clients can connect to any copy directly.
Autoscalers can only start and stop stateless containers; stateful ones need manual scaling.

explanation: Because no server owns unique data, the platform can add copies under load and remove them later without migrating or destroying anything. (a) is unrelated: CPU and memory depend on the work, not on where state lives. (c) is false; you still need something to spread traffic and remove failed copies. (d) is false; autoscalers can start anything, the problem is what you lose when they stop a stateful instance.

scenario: You moved sessions to Redis and removed sticky routing. A week later, Redis restarts during a maintenance window with persistence turned off.
prompt: What happens, and what is the lesson?

options.text: Nothing changes for users; stateless app servers are immune because they never held the sessions.
Every user is logged out; the state moved to Redis, so Redis now needs replication or persistence.
Only users whose requests were pinned to one particular app server are logged out; the rest are fine.
Sessions are rebuilt automatically from the load balancer's routing table, so users stay logged in.

explanation: Moving state does not remove it. The session store is now the stateful component, so its durability matters: use a replica, persistence, or accept that a restart logs everyone out. (a) ignores where the state went: the app servers are stateless precisely because Redis holds the sessions. (c) describes the old in-memory sticky design; with Redis every user's session was in the restarted store. (d) is false; load balancers do not keep session data.

prompt: Which of these is a good use of an app server's local memory?

options.text: The only copy of each user's shopping cart, since reading it from local RAM avoids a network hop
A copy of feature-flag settings that is refreshed every 30 seconds from a central store
Progress of large uploads, which must survive a deploy so users can resume where they stopped
Payment records awaiting settlement, held in memory so the nightly batch job can read them fast

explanation: Memory is for copies, not for the only copy. A refreshed copy of feature flags can be rebuilt after a restart. (a), (c) and (d) are the only copies of data that matters: saving a network hop or a fast batch read is not worth losing carts or payments on a restart, and upload progress held in memory cannot survive a deploy by definition.

prompt: Sticky sessions cause which problems? Select all that apply.

options.text: Uneven load when some users are much heavier than others
Users lose in-memory sessions when their server restarts
New servers only receive new users, so they cannot absorb load from existing users
Requests become slower because the load balancer must query the database

explanation: Pinning users to servers skews load, ties session lifetime to server lifetime, and limits how fast new capacity helps. (d) is wrong: sticky routing is usually done with a cookie or a hash of the client IP, without a database query.
